title: Judah's Longest and Worst Reign
overview: King Manasseh undoes his father's religious reforms, fills Jerusalem with other gods and violence, and is told the city will fall; his son Amon follows him and is murdered.

parts.label: Manasseh reverses his father (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Crowned at twelve, Manasseh rebuilt the hilltop shrines his father Hezekiah had torn down and brought in worship of Baal (a Canaanite storm god), Asherah (a goddess honored with a wooden pole) and the sun, moon and stars. He even set up altars to these in the temple's two courtyards.

parts.label: Fire and fortune-telling (v. 6)
parts.note: The text says he made his son "pass through the fire," which many scholars read as child sacrifice, though others think it may describe a dedication ritual, and the wording is debated. He also relied on omens, fortune-tellers and people who claimed to speak with the dead.

parts.label: Idols inside the temple (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: Setting up the Asherah pole inside the temple is singled out as the worst offense, because this was the place where God had promised to put his Name. The promise that Israel would stay in its land depended on keeping the law of Moses, and the writer says Judah now did worse than the nations who lived there before.

parts.label: The prophets announce ruin (vv. 10-15)
parts.note: The measuring line and plumb line were builders' tools, used here for tearing down: Jerusalem will be judged like Samaria, the northern capital already destroyed, and like King Ahab's wiped out family. Wiping a dish and turning it upside down pictures the city emptied completely, which the writer sees fulfilled later when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem.

parts.label: A city full of blood (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: Manasseh also killed many innocent people, though the text does not say who. Later Jewish tradition claimed the prophet Isaiah was among them, but the Bible itself does not say so.

parts.label: Amon's short reign (vv. 19-26)
parts.note: His son Amon kept the same practices and was murdered by his own officials after two years. The "people of the land," probably the landowning citizens of Judah, killed the plotters and made his young son Josiah king.

disagreement: Readers differ on how to fit this harsh portrait with 2 Chronicles 33, which says Manasseh later repented, and on whether his reign alone sealed Judah's fall or was the last straw in a longer story.
think: Manasseh's choices shaped a whole nation for decades; how much do you think one leader is responsible for what the people around them become?
